1077-the-mirror-of-kong-ho:
Ernest Bramah invents Kong Ho, a Chinese gentleman who writes home about England with grave courtesy and total misunderstanding. Trains, teapots, policemen, and English manners all pass through his polite, literal gaze, and the result is satire aimed at both East and West. The letters first ran as a series.

Kong Ho's formal English and his Confucian maxims turn London life upside down, and his mishaps grow funnier as he grows bolder. Bramah, famed for his Kai Lung tales, writes here with a lighter, more mocking hand. The book charms readers who enjoy wit that cuts both ways.
12138-the-history-of-university-educatio:
The History of University Education in Maryland, in the Johns Hopkins University Studies in Historical and Political Science, edited by Herbert B. Adams, pairs two works: Bernard C. Steiner's history, and Daniel C. Gilman's Johns Hopkins University, 1876 to 1891, with supplementary notes. Steiner, a Yale fellow in history, and Gilman, president of the university, write from inside the institution they describe.

The volume traces Maryland's colleges and the founding of Johns Hopkins as a research university, a new model for American higher education. For historians of education, it preserves the arguments, benefactions, and experiments that shaped a university designed for graduate study and original research.
14546-betty-gordon-at-mountain-camp-or-t:
Alice B. Emerson's Betty Gordon at Mountain Camp, with the mystery of Ida Bellethorne, sends Betty and her friends to a mountain camp for girls. Cupples and Leon published the illustrated volume for girls.

Ida, a girl who has lost her place with Mrs. Staples, puzzles Betty, while Bobby and Bob Henderson debate a lost locket and a mistake Ida has made. Camp fun, hikes, and detective work fill the chapters. The book is a wholesome girls' series tale, brisk and kindly, in the Ruth Fielding tradition Emerson also wrote.
15904-the-rover-boys-on-the-river-or-the:
A Rover Boys story by Arthur Winfield, on the river and the search for a missing houseboat. Plans for an outing lead back to Putnam Hall, where night doings and a morning's news stir trouble. Link Smith's confession and fun on the campus fill the school chapters. Winfield writes for boys who loved the series' mix of school and adventure.

Good-bye to Putnam Hall sends the boys home, then aboard a houseboat for days of pleasure. Flapp and Baxter plot mischief, a queer captain appears, and the houseboat vanishes. Words and blows follow as the boys hunt their boat. The tale pleases as a river adventure: chums, crooks, and a mystery afloat.
1593-how-to-tell-the-birds-from-the-flow:
Robert Williams Wood's Manual of Flornithology for Beginners, published by Paul Elder and Company in 1907, is a book of jokes in verse and picture. Each page pairs a bird with a flower it resembles, from a catbird to a pussywillow, and asks the reader to tell one from the other by rhyme and drawing.

Wood, a physicist with a playful pen, delights in puns and look-alikes, and the illustrations carry half the humour. The book is slight, silly, and charming. It is a period piece of American whimsy, best enjoyed as a gift book for nature lovers with a taste for wordplay.
18170-the-excellence-of-the-rosary-confe:
Rev. M. J. Frings wrote these conferences for devotions in honor of the Blessed Virgin, published in New York in 1912 with the approval of Cardinal Farley. The book explains the rosary as a form of prayer, conference by conference, for use in sodalities and parish devotions. Its opening cites Pope Pius IX urging pilgrims to fight persecution with the rosary, prayer, and good example.

Conferences take up the name of the devotion, its origin, its power, the sign of the cross, the Apostles' Creed, the Glory Be, the Our Father, and the Hail Mary. Later talks treat the form of the rosary and the mysteries it recalls. Catholics get a plain guide to praying the rosary with understanding, and to why each prayer holds its place.
18770-a-christmas-story-man-in-his-eleme:
Dr. Samuel W. Francis published this Christmas story with George H. Mathews of New York in 1867, under the second title Man in His Element, or A New Way to Keep House. Its narrator William, an old bachelor, hears his widowed sister Mary's long complaint about servants, stores, and soap.

Mary envies the boarding house they left, where no chasing after girls, candles, linen, or coachmen ate her days. She mourns a pair of gaiters she gave Jane, found the next morning in the ash barrel. William answers that he can put the matter in a new light, and Mary doubts any man was ever convinced by a woman. The tale promises a bachelor's plan for keeping house without the daily war of servants.
25012-the-case-of-wagner-nietzsche-contr:
Friedrich Nietzsche's two essays on Wagner, translated by Anthony M. Ludovici, third edition, from T. N. Foulis, pair The Case of Wagner: A Musician's Problem with Nietzsche contra Wagner, plus aphorisms from his retrospect of friendship with Wagner. The translator dates the Case to Turin in May 1888, completed at Sils Maria that June and published the following autumn. Nietzsche contra Wagner, written in mid December 1888, and corrected before the New Year, waited long for publication after Nietzsche's breakdown in early 1889.

Ludovici warns readers not to mistake the essays' virulent tone for a cover for personal feud or envy of Wagner in his glory. He warns against supposing the issue is religion rather than music. Nietzsche's charge, developed in the text, is that Wagner's music no longer lives: composed, reckoned, artificial, a fictitious thing, built from attitudes first and tones second. The volume is white hot polemic.
30094-fred-fenton-marathon-runner-the-gr:
Allen Chapman wrote Fred Fenton, Marathon Runner, subtitled The Great Race at Riverport School. Twenty-five chapters carry the school story, opening in the snow with a shooting contest at a round hole in a tree trunk, twenty yards away, or twenty-five by Bristles's measure. Fred Fenton, regular pitcher on the Riverside High School nine, is barred as handicapped, since he is used to putting them over the plate for a steady diet.

 Looking over the course, the wild dog pack, and the short-cut way lead to the tell-tale pin and the toll-gate. Bristles's surprise party, the green campus, and laying plans give way to the muffled voice and a plot that failed. Clinching evidence, lining up for the trial spin, and a storm lead to the circus at Riverport, the greatest of days, and the marathon runners.
31773-si-klegg-book-3-si-and-shorty-meet:
John McElroy's third Si Klegg book, in its second edition of 1910, is titled for the meeting of Si and Shorty with Mr. Rosenbaum, the spy who relates his adventures. It opens with Si in charge of a picket post on the Readyville Pike near Cripple Deer Creek. The Deacon, fidgety to get back to his own fields, wanted to see picket duty.

The Deacon's visit brings comedy: Abraham Lincoln, left behind to care for the house, has shown no strong qualities except eating and sleeping in unlimited quantities. Readers get another volume of Civil War camp humor, mixing picket duty, spies, and the Deacon's blunders with the daily life of the 200th Indiana.
3268-the-mysteries-of-udolpho:
Ann Radcliffe's great gothic romance runs to three volumes in this edition, with poems interspersed through the prose. Emily St Aubert, orphaned and tender, passes into the power of the villain Montoni and his castle of Udolpho, high in the Apennines. Veiled pictures, midnight music, and locked doors supply the terrors, all in Radcliffe's rich, scenic prose.

The mysteries, famously, admit natural explanations in the end, but the dread they raise is real while it lasts. Radcliffe invented the female gothic here: a heroine whose sensibility is both her danger and her defense. Readers who enjoy castles, villains, and sublime landscape will find the original pattern, imitated ever since and never quite outdone.
33984-the-man-from-jericho:
Edwin Carlile Litsey wrote this Kentucky novel, published in New York in 1911 by the Neale Publishing Company. Litsey dedicates the book to Padre Francois, humanitarian and friend. The story opens after a thunder-shower, when sun breaks over a drenched Kentucky landscape of bluegrass, ponds, nasturtiums, and trumpet-vines.

Orioles weave flame among oak boughs, and honey-bees rise to seek distant sweets. Litsey writes the Kentucky country with lush, loving detail and with a poet's eye for light after rain. The novel offers a period tale of the bluegrass, told in a rich, old-fashioned voice.
34016-unc-edinburg-a-plantation-echo:
Thomas Nelson Page wrote this plantation tale, published in New York in 1897 by Charles Scribner's Sons, with pictures by B. West Clinedinst. The narrator, bound for Werrowcoke to spend Christmas, meets Unc' Edinburg at the station on Christmas Eve. Edinburg, a ragged old driver with a great cedar-staffed whip and a calico letter-bag, drives the muddiest road in eastern Virginia.

Page tells the story through Edinburg's voice, with Marse George, Miss Charlotte, and a carriage at its heart. The tale is a Christmas echo of the old plantation South, told with humor and feeling. It remains a period piece of Virginia storytelling.
35205-who:
Elizabeth Kent's mystery novel, issued by Putnam's Sons in New York and London in 1912, begins on a raw October morning at Newhaven. Cyril Crichton lands from the cross-Channel boat after three years away, resolved to make no more a fool of himself. He goes to wire his friend Campbell, finds the telegraph office shut until eight, and races back to a train already moving.

The chapters promise a woman in the compartment, a scene of tragedy, an inquest, jewels, and finger prints in the dust. Campbell detects, remonstrates, and at last resigns, while Cyril makes a perilous venture and slips his tongue. The contents end with two chapters called What Is the Truth and The Truth, and the frontispiece shows a cry: quick, I hear footsteps on the stairs.
35968-a-check-list-of-the-birds-of-idaho:
A Check-List of the Birds of Idaho is a science paper by Dale Arvey. The University of Kansas Museum of Natural History issued the paper. It stands as volume one, number ten, pages 193 to 216. The paper came out on November 29, in the year 1947. Ferd Voiland, state printer at Topeka, printed the Kansas journal part.

Little literature deals with the birds of Idaho, Arvey opens frankly. Few persons had done field work in the state before his stay. No state list existed to tell whether a bird was new there. Arvey collected in Idaho from October 1938 to September 1944 himself. Published reports he could find stand drawn upon beside his own notes. For each species he gives at least one record of date and place. The list aims to stir additions and corrections from other hands.
36584-the-blind-beggar-of-jericho:
The Blind Beggar of Jericho, number thirty-five in its tract series, was published by Hatchard at London in 1848. Its author is named only as the author of Peep of Day. A blind man sits begging by the roadside and hears a great crowd passing. Told that Jesus of Nazareth is going by, he cries out for mercy again and again. The crowd rebukes him, but he cries the more, knowing Jesus may never pass that way again.

Jesus stands still and calls him, asking what he wishes. Sight, the beggar answers, and his eyes are touched and opened at once. He follows Jesus down the road, praising God. The tract then turns straight to the child who reads it. You are not blind, it says, but there is something Jesus can do for you too.
36694-the-lay-man-s-sermon-upon-the-late:
The Lay-Man's Sermon upon the Late Storm is a short tract by Daniel Defoe, printed in 1704 after a great storm. It claims to have been held forth at an honest coffee house gathering. The text takes its theme from the book of Nahum, where the Lord is said to have his way in the whirlwind and the storm.

Defoe reads the verse as words about Nineveh, a rich and proud city under God's charge. He argues that God is slow to anger with his own people yet stern with the wicked. The tract turns a fresh disaster into a call for sober thought, in the sharp prose Defoe was known for.
40415-tower-s-little-primer-for-the-youn:
Tower's Little Primer is a first reading book for the youngest class in primary schools, by Anna Tower. Brown, Taggard and Chase published it at Boston in 1857. Its preface explains the method. Only a few letters at a time are given to the pupil, with words formed of those few letters.

Each new portion of the alphabet is used in words before the next is learned. No word appears in the reading until it has first come in a spelling lesson. Alphabets at the front serve teachers who prefer the old order. The primer leads into the Gradual Primer, the first reader of Tower's series. It shows how reading was taught letter by letter in the eighteen fifties.
40462-it-was-the-road-to-jericho:
Annie Fellows Johnston, author of The Little Colonel, published It Was the Road to Jericho in 1919, with illustrations by John Neill, the illustrator of Oz. The book retells the parable of the good Samaritan in verse.

The road to Jericho was a brave road to walk alone, where robber hordes swooped down the cliffs like eagles on their prey and mercy was not known to them. A man riding by hears a groan of mortal pain. He gets down from his beast and finds the one who bled where the thieves had bruised and beaten him. Johnston turns the parable into a ballad for the young, in the year after a war that had filled roads with the wounded and made the Samaritan's choice a daily one.
42214-on-a-donkey-s-hurricane-deck-a-tem:
R Pitcher Woodward, writing as Pythagoras Pod, rode a donkey across the American continent and wrote this comic account of the trip, published in 1902 with thirty-nine photos taken on the way. The title page gives the measure of the feat: four thousand and ninety-six miles, in 340 days and 2 hours, starting without a dollar.

The contents promise polishing shoes at Vassar, mopping a hotel floor, sleeping in a haymow below zero, and crossing the Mississippi and the Missouri. Later come Pike's Peak, a rattlesnake bite, a cyclone, and snow in the Sierras, ending with San Francisco at last. Readers get a cheerful stunt journey, told for laughs.
42358-frank-at-don-carlos-rancho:
Harry Castlemon's Frank at Don Carlos' Rancho, a volume of the Rocky Mountain Series from Porter and Coates of Philadelphia, continues the adventures of Frank and Archie Winters in California. Seventeen chapters promise bear hunts, a running fight, a heavy reward and a race in the dark. The boys, seasoned by Arthur Vane and Pierre Costello's band, admit they have had more perilous adventure than they wanted.

The opening chapter, All about Horses, finds Frank, Archie, Dick Thomas and Johnny Harris shut inside a room at Mr Winters's rancho. With every opening but the port-holes closed against danger, the boys sweat through a tense council.
43929-the-collector-essays-on-books-news:
Henry Tuckerman's The Collector gathers essays on books, newspapers, pictures, inns, authors, doctors, holidays, actors, and preachers. John Camden Hotten of Piccadilly published it in London, with an introduction by Doran, the author of Table Traits and History of Court Fools. The contents add lawyers, sepulchres, statues, and bridges to the title's list.

Doran's introduction opens with books themselves, the means by which language outruns its natural bounds and letters waft a sigh from Indus to the Pole. He then takes up the first essay, on inns, and the great change in London taverns after the death of James the First. Tavern licences at three pounds a year, he notes, let keepers charge what they pleased, to many a thirsty Cockney's cost.
44694-pearse-s-commercial-directory-to-s:
Pearse made a trade list book for Swansea and the towns near it for 1854. Pearse sold books and print work in Swansea. The book lists trades, shops, and homes in A-to-Z and class order. It also lists town staff, post times, and mail rules. David Price typed this copy from the 1854 book.

A front part praises the town's bay, hills, and mild air off the sea. It calls Swansea the first trade town in Wales. The main lists let a reader find a shop, a clerk, or a home fast. Such books are gold for those who trace kin or trade.
44846-the-motor-boys-on-the-atlantic-or-:
The Motor Boys on the Atlantic, or The Mystery of the Lighthouse, is a boys' tale by Clarence Young. Young was the author of the Racer Boys and Jack Ranger series. The book came out in New York from Cupples and Leon Company, dated 1908 in the pack. A picture at its front shows half a steamer sunk from sight beneath the waves.

The front pages list the books of the Motor Boys Series. The Motor Boys, or Chums Through Thick and Thin, stands first. The Motor Boys Overland, In Mexico, Across the Plains, and Afloat stand in the list. On the Atlantic and In Strange Waters stand there too, as the list breaks off. The tale at hand joins the chums' motor boat life to a mystery of a lighthouse on the coast, as its twin titles state.
45872-pretty-geraldine-the-new-york-sale:
Pretty Geraldine, the New York Salesgirl, is a story paper novel by Mrs Alex McVeigh Miller. Street and Smith issued it as number thirty four of the Eagle Library at ten cents. That weekly series boasted paper and printing equal to any twenty five cent line. A handsome cover of fresh design graced each issue of the set.

The Eagle Library called itself the most popular series of novels then published. Its books were copyrighted stories that could be had in no other edition. A salesgirl heroine in New York, wedded to her choice as the subtitle hints, fits the line. Romance for working girls was a strong seller in the eighteen nineties market. Miller wrote many such tales of shop girls, trials, and love rewarded.
46300-the-first-canadians-in-france-the-:
First Canadians in France chronicles a Canadian military hospital in the war zone. McKelvey Bell wrote it, with pictures drawn by Christopher Fulleylove. Toronto houses issued it, with rights held in 1917 by Doran. Bell dedicates the pages to Surgeon General Guy Carleton Jones by name. He also dedicates them to the Canadian Medical Services overseas as a body.

Bell praises skilled guidance that gave that service a top status. The sick and wounded soldier, he says, found there a home. His preface faults himself for too little stress on the ranks. Non commissioned officers and men showed heroism and self sacrifice, he writes. Readers get the daily life of a hospital close behind the lines.
46968-the-boy-scouts-on-war-trails-in-be:
The Boy Scouts on War Trails in Belgium, by Herbert Carter, was held under a 1916 copyright by A L Burt Company. Its second title is Caught Between Hostile Armies. Carter wrote many Boy Scout tales, from the Blue Ridge to the Maine woods.

Early chapters bring news to the Rhine, a bold plan, and a bargain made by Giraffe. The scouts find the way to the border blocked, take a ferry, and use scout tactics to dodge trouble. Later heads name a Belgian inn, a warning off, and a penalty for meddling. A front plate shows Thad urged to squeeze more speed from a poor old car. Boys of the war years got scouting skill set in a live war zone.
46973-the-maya-indians-of-southern-yucat:
Thomas Gann wrote this ethnology bulletin for the Smithsonian Institution, printed at Washington in 1918. Bulletin 64 of the Bureau of American Ethnology carries his memoir on the Maya. A letter of transmittal from Hodge, dated November 4, 1916, sends the manuscript to Secretary Walcott with a warm recommendation.

Part one treats customs, ceremonies and mode of life among the Maya of the region. Habitat, personal characteristics, dress and work open Gann's contents in that part. Agriculture, food and cooking, hunting, fishing and house building follow, with pottery making and boat building among the crafts described by a doctor who lived among his subjects.
47537-the-marquis-d-argenson-a-study-in-:
Arthur Ogle wrote The Marquis d'Argenson, the Stanhope Essay of Oxford, 1893, printed in London that year. Contents fall in four spans of years. The first, 1630 to 1721, treats the father: a friend of Richelieu and Mazarin, an unlucky envoy, and a great chief of police.

The second span, 1694 to 1724, gives the son as a man of the world. It treats his schooldays, his entry into public life, and his post as director of the press. D'Argenson in battle with the Parlement against the schemes of Law, and Law's arrest by him, follow. The third span, to 1744, gives the Club de l'Entresol, its stamping out, and a would-be statesman's thwarted hopes. It treats his feud with Cardinal Fleury and his letters with Voltaire. The last span covers his years as foreign minister.
47549-bonnie-scotland-painted-by-sutton-:
Bonnie Scotland pairs colour pictures by Sutton Palmer with text by Hope Moncrieff. The book first came out in 1904 and was reprinted in 1912. In his note, the author says he will not try to match the paint with fine words.

He offers an outline of Scotland's chief features, with glimpses of its past and its customs. The tour stays on the mainland and runs from the Borders to John o' Groat's House. Chapters take in Edinburgh, the Trossachs, Fife, Glasgow and Galloway. Tales and memories are woven in to keep the trip lively for fireside readers. A full list of Palmer's plates shows how much of the book rests on his art.
50377-memoirs-of-the-generals-commodores:
Thomas Wyatt honours medal-winning officers of two wars in a Carey and Hart volume from Philadelphia dated MDCCCXLVIII. Eighty-two steel engravings from the medals themselves show each award in full. Rights were held from 1847, and T K and P G Collins printed the work in Lodge Alley.

Wyatt states in his preface that Americans will view the national stamp of such a work with pride. Lives of generals, commodores, and other commanders who won medals from Congress fill the pages. Their deeds span the Revolution and the War of 1812, when the might of the mistress of the seas was matched at last. Like old Rome, Wyatt argues, America opens public honours to the virtue of each citizen who serves her well.
5171-thomas-hariot-the-mathematician-the:
Henry Stevens's study gathers what could be known in the nineteenth century about Thomas Hariot, the Elizabethan mathematician, philosopher, and scholar. Hariot's only published works were his Briefe and True Report on Virginia and a posthumous algebra. He also observed comets, corresponded with Kepler, and anticipated the law of refraction.

Stevens prints letters, including Hariot's correspondence with Sir William Lower at Sion. He adds biographical and bibliographical notes on Hariot's associates. The book serves as a record of a brilliant, half-lost scientific life. It remains useful for readers interested in the quiet scholars behind the age of exploration.
52069-lives-of-boulton-and-watt-principa:
Lives of Boulton and Watt gives the joint story of the two men who made the steam engine a business. The author had written Lives of British Engineers and the famed Self Help before it. A list of those works fills the front pages of this volume. Portraits and hundreds of woodcuts went with the set.

Matthew Boulton of the Soho works and James Watt, the improver of steam, stand paired here. The lives are drawn principally from the original papers at Soho. That archive gives the book its weight as a source. Industry, patents, and partnership fill the tale of the two Scots and English makers. The volume belongs to the great Victorian line of lives of engineers. It shows invention as a matter of workshops, money, and grit.
53648-trip-to-the-west-and-texas-compris:
Parker wrote an account of a long trip through the west and Texas, in a second edition issued in 1836. Parker rode eight thousand miles in the autumn and winter of 1834-5, through New-York, Michigan, Illinois, Missouri, Louisiana, and Texas. He spent five months on the road.

Parker says he tells a plain tale in his own way, with no reach for fancy or fiction. He notes soil, weather, crops, health, beasts, and the habits of the folk he met. An appendix gives a full sketch of Michigan and a brief account of the Texian war, drawn from all the reports he could find.
57471-a-settler-s-35-years-experience-in:
A settler's account fills this pamphlet: A Settler's 35 Years' Experience in Victoria, Australia, printed at Melbourne. Its title page carries a boast in figures, telling how a few pounds became eight thousand, and promises advice to settlers. The book is inscribed, by permission, to Alfred Deakin, chief secretary of Victoria.

Contents trace the whole arc. An artist's life and a farewell to England lead to Melbourne, the diggings, and ten years there, then farming and growing holdings. Later pieces treat temperance, the vine industry, irrigation, and a scheme of settlement. The writer says he speaks to working men and gentlefolk alike in the crowded old country, and above all to those with large families and little hope.
57760-from-boniface-to-bank-burglar-or-t:
George White, alias George Bliss, wrote From Boniface to Bank Burglar, or The Price of Persecution, printed in Vermont in 1905. White tells how a successful business man, through a failure of justice, became a notorious bank looter. Part one covers his hotel days, the Walpole bank burglary, sheriffs, and persecution.

Part two runs through Whitecaps, the Cadiz bank loot, a corrupted bank clerk, and a colossal bank burgling enterprise. Chapters treat prison, plots against a captain, a patent safety switch, and the Ocean Bank loot division among the gang. White writes as an insider with a grievance against the law that pursued him. True crime readers get a raw outlaw memoir.
60906-sappho:
Tucker's Sappho is a lecture delivered before the Classical Association of Victoria in 1913 and printed at Melbourne in 1914. Tucker held the chair of classical philology at the University of Melbourne. He begins with the background: Lesbos about the year 600 before Christ. The island, now called Mytilini, is a rounded triangle pierced on the south by two deep fiords. It stretches some thirty-five miles one way and twenty-five the other.

From its northern shore Sappho could see the Troad, seven miles off, and many-fountained Ida beyond. Tucker praises the clear air, the mild climate, and soil rich in corn, oil, wine, figs, and olives. Lesbos was a land of flowers, loved as flowers are loved in Japan. Alcaeus and a whole school of finished lyric poetry shared the island with her. The Aeolian Greeks of Lesbos are set against the slower Saxon-like Spartans.
62260-trouble-on-tycho:
Nelson S Bond sends a weather man with a set of squeeze-pipes to the Moon in a tale from Planet Stories for March 1943. A head note calls Isobar Jones and his pipes the bane of the Moon Station. A day will come when his worth lies in that very nuisance, the note adds.

Isobar takes a call from Dome Commander Colonel Eagan on the audiophone and grumbles at his lot. He has marked ditto signs under Clear for six months in his observation log, he grants with gloom. Sun spot counts and neat curves on an Earth chart fill his dull daily sheet at Tycho. Eagan cuts him off mid-plea for his bag, and Isobar says nuts to the dead plate.
6393-the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-vol:
Ferentum in Etruria gives Otho his ancestors, an ancient and honourable family among the most considerable of the region. His grandfather, son of a Roman knight and a mother of uncertain birth, was educated in Livia Augusta's house and rose to praetor but no higher. His father Lucius, nobly descended on his mother's side and dearly beloved by Tiberius, so resembled the emperor in features that most people believed a closer tie.

A. Salvius Otho's own rise turns on omens, the advice of Seleucus, and a signal word from a freedman about architects come, agreed beforehand. Waiting accomplices stand in the Forum by Saturn's temple at the gilded milestone, while Otho pays respects to Galba, hears the augur, and moves. Suetonius writes a short reign begun in conspiracy, where birth, favour, and timing decide an empire in a morning.
65234-1851-or-the-adventures-of-mr-and-m:
1851, or The Adventures of Mr and Mrs Cursty Sandboys, is a comic tale of the Great Exhibition year. George Newbold published it at London, on the Strand. George Cruikshank designed and etched the ten plates. The frontispiece shows all the world going to see the Great Exhibition. Other plates show the family looking for lodgings, the first shilling-day, and London crammed while Manchester stands deserted.

The dispersion of the works of all nations closes the plate list. The first chapter opens with a Cumberland song, Nichol the Newsmonger, in dialect. The Exhibition is about to attract the sight-seers of all the world, the narrator says. The African has mounted his ostrich, and excursion caravans are announced. A country family loose in exhibition London was rich material in 1851. Cruikshank's plates carry half the joke.
67379-a-cyclop-dia-of-sacred-poetical-qu:
A Cyclopaedia of Sacred Poetical Quotations gathers devotional verse under subject heads. Adams edited the book as a companion to his earlier Cyclopaedia of Poetical Quotations. Gardner published this new edition at Paisley and London. Portraits of Herbert, Milton, Young, and Cowper face the title page.

Adams explains that calls for more of the plan led to this volume. Every piece here is sacred in character, where the first book mixed all kinds. Longer poems find room, since the heads are fewer. Scripture passages stand beside the poems to light them up. Adams sought to keep the book free of party doctrine. Milton, Watts, Wesley, and Keble all supply verses. The volume served preachers and families hunting a apt sacred line.
67673-recollections-the-reminiscences-of:
Recollections holds the memories of the busy life of one who has played the varied parts of sailor, author, and lecturer. Frank T Bullen wrote it, and Seeley, Service and Company printed it in London in 1915. A portrait stands at the front. Bullen list of works runs to more than thirty sea books, led by The Cruise of the Cachalot.

Chapters open with his earliest memories and random memories, then his first lectures and a lecture tour. The real beginning, Scotland, and later parts follow. Bullen jokes in his opening that some readers never read a preface or an opening by any chance. He tells of reading a volume of memories where the writer made the same point. Sea fans get the life tale of a whaler turned famed writer and speaker.
67878-gods-of-modern-grub-street-impress:
A St John Adcock profiles living British authors in a volume issued in New York in 1923. Thirty-two portraits after photos by E O Hoppe face the chapters. The roster runs from Thomas Hardy and Rudyard Kipling to H G Wells and A A Milne.

Inside, each chapter gives a short, frank sketch of one writer's work, fame, and place in current letters. The Hardy chapter argues that harsh reviews helped end Hardy the novelist and cleared the way for Hardy the poet. Other subjects include Arnold Bennett, John Galsworthy, Arthur Conan Doyle, and Somerset Maugham. Readers get a lively snapshot of the British literary scene as one working critic saw it in the early nineteen twenties.
68910-the-history-of-bannock-county-idah:
Arthur Saunders wrote The History of Bannock County, Idaho, in 1915. The Tribune company at Pocatello published the county history. Contents open with an introduction and a preliminary history. Some natural history and the Indians take the next chapters. The cowboy, Fort Hall, and two Indian wars follow in the list.

The Nez Perce war and the Bannock war fill chapters six and seven. The stage coach and the railroad carry the tale forward in time. General conditions and development, and Pocatello itself, come late. Chapter one opens in 1662 with La Salle planting a flag. Louisiana, named for Louis the Fourteenth, frames the county's start. Cession to Spain, a sale to Napoleon, and Jefferson's purchase follow. Fifteen million dollars bought that territory in 1803, it says. Gray and Kendrick skirted its coast for furs in 1789.
6918-the-history-of-the-reign-of-ferdina:
William Prescott tells the reign of Ferdinand and Isabella the Catholic in three volumes, and this is the first. He dedicates the work to his father, William Prescott, guide of his youth and best friend in riper years, with warm filial affection. His preface notes that English writers had covered Spanish reigns from Charles the Fifth onward, yet no full account of this earlier turning point existed.

Prescott therefore takes up the Catholic monarchs whose rule joined Spain and opened a new age for Europe. The volume opens the story with the state of the peninsula and the forces that shaped the reign. Later volumes carry the tale forward, but this first book lays the ground for a history long praised for learning and for narrative power.
6967-the-history-of-the-reign-of-ferdina:
Prescott's second volume on Ferdinand and Isabella continues the reign with the internal affairs of the kingdom and the war in Granada. Chapter twelve treats the Inquisition in Aragon, Isabella enforcing the laws, the marriage of Catharine of Navarre, the freeing of Catalan serfs, and the remonstrances of the Cortes. A conspiracy and the murder of Arbues lead to cruel persecutions across Ferdinand's dominions.

Chapter thirteen turns to war, with the surrender of Velez Malaga, the siege and conquest of Malaga, and the narrow escape of Ferdinand himself. The queen visits the camp, the town is summoned, and civil feuds among the Moors shape the fight. Only this second volume's matter is described here, in Prescott's learned and vivid narrative.
6968-the-history-of-the-reign-of-ferdina:
Prescott's third volume on Ferdinand and Isabella turns to the Italian wars and the partition of Naples. Chapter ten follows Louis the Twelfth's designs on Italy, the French conquest of Milan, alarm at the Spanish court, and bold remonstrance to the Pope. Gonsalvo de Cordova sails with a fleet, the partition of Naples is confirmed by the Pope, and Italy stands astonished at French success and cruelty.

Gonsalvo then overruns Calabria, invests Tarento, punishes a mutiny, and presses a bolder plan of attack, despite discontents in his army. Only this third volume's matter is described here, from the Italian campaigns onward. Prescott writes with the same command of sources and narrative pace that mark the whole history.
70272-the-theory-of-relativity-and-its-i:
The Theory of Relativity and Its Influence on Scientific Thought is a lecture by Arthur Stanley Eddington. He delivered it as the Romanes Lecture at Oxford in 1922. The Sheldonian Theatre heard it on the twenty fourth of May. The Clarendon Press published the text the same year. Eddington was Plumian Professor of Astronomy at Cambridge. He also presided over the Royal Astronomical Society then.

A passage from Carlyle's Sartor Resartus stands as the motto. The lecture opens before Copernicus, with earth as the hub of the universe. Planets looped in epicycles, and spheres turned within spheres. Copernicus changed the view point, and the simple solar system appeared. Eddington traces how Einstein's theory works a like change of view. Where and when, he argues, are not the fixed frame men assumed.
72526-madame-goubaud-s-pillow-lace-patte:
Madame Goubaud’s Pillow Lace Patterns and Instructions teaches bobbin lace work. The Goubaud name stood on a row of needlework books of the day. Tatting, crochet, knitting, and point lace fill her trade list. Her larger Pillow Lace book sold at three shillings and sixpence.

Berlin work and monogram books share the one shilling shelf line. Trimmed paper patterns of the newest modes came by post from her shop. Thirty Henrietta Street in Covent Garden took those ladies’ orders. Beeton’s Household Books are praised on the same gay pages here. Mrs Beeton’s Household Management heads that famed home shelf. Wedding outfits and baby linen crowd the next bright notice. Whole sets for India, China, Japan, and Australia stand priced there. Tartan plaids from Inverness close the roll of trade plates.
73125-the-black-panther-of-the-navaho:
The Black Panther of the Navaho is an adventure novel by Warren Miller, published in 1921. Appleton issued it at New York and London. Miller had written hunting books for boys before it. Twelve chapters cross the Southwest. The wonderland of the Southwest opens the tale, then the Painted Desert. The valley of the cliff dwellers and Lost Canyon follow. The claws of the black panther strike in chapter five.

A fire dance of the Navaho and a Kaibab grizzly raise the middle. White Mesa and the panther's last stand close the contents. The story opens in Colonel Colvin's trophy den at home. The old Indian fighter sits worn and gray after wartime desk duty in Washington. His son Sid and Sid's chum Scotty mend moccasins nearby. Sid fears a collapse unless his father returns to outdoor life.
73565-carlota-of-the-rancho:
Carlota of the Rancho is a girls' novel by Evelyn Raymond. The Penn Publishing Company issued it in Philadelphia in 1909. Sarah A Shreve drew the illustrations. Raymond had earlier written Polly the Gringo and My Lady Barefoot. The story opens on the border land between the United States and Mexico. Twins Carlos and Carlota play on the line itself.

Carlos sprawls on the grass with his head in one country and his feet in the other. Carlota rolls across the lime-line to beat him, heart in her own country. Old Marta, the housekeeper of the adobe house, comes to the door at their laughter. Nobody knows Marta's real age, and she keeps the heart of a child. The chapter titles promise a rancho life of guests, storms, and rides. A norther, a first ride on the railway, and the siege of Cork lie ahead.
77313-a-sailor-boy-s-log-book-from-ports:
A Sailor-Boy's Log-Book: From Portsmouth to the Peiho, edited by Walter White, was published by Chapman and Hall at London in 1862. White's foreword vouches for the book: it is the work of one who entered the navy as a boy and kept a log through his service.

The boy sailed to China, smelt powder at the capture of Canton and the disastrous attempt on the Taku forts, visited Japan, and came home a smart young topman. Sea-life here is told from the lower deck, not the quarter-deck, with a boy's fresh disregard of consequences.
79692-the-famous-killer-who:
The Famous Killer Who is a western story by Ray Humphreys. Humphreys also wrote The Very Outlaw He Was. The tale opens in the town of Monte Vista. Sheriff Joe Cook takes a fat cigar from the mayor. His deputy, Shorty McKay, is the sheriff's sore point. Shorty haunts the railroad station at noon. A pretty girl telegrapher there draws him like a magnet.

The sheriff growls that he is not against women in business. He is against pretty ones mixing business and romance. A stray horse errand sent Shorty past the station. The noon train's arrival is the magnet's hour. Dialect speech carries much of the humour. Western pulps ran on such small-town sparks. A killer of fame waits behind the comic opening. The title itself breaks off like a headline.
9616-ramuntcho:
Pierre Loti wrote Ramuntcho, a novel of the Basque country, here in Henri Pene du Bois's translation. Ramuntcho, a young mountaineer, walks home through autumn rain toward his shaded house near the Spanish frontier. Curlews cry over cold rivers, the Adour, Nivelle, and Bidassoa, as October night falls. Loti paints Pyrenean woods, moss paths, and rope-soled tread with lyrical care.

The novel follows Ramuntcho's love, smuggling, and fate on a border where France meets Spain. Loti's prose favors mood, landscape, and the ache of parting. A reader gets a haunting Basque romance, rich in sea, mountain, and the melancholy of declining seasons.
a-christmas-story-man-in-his-element-or-: Samuel Ward Francis tells a Christmas story subtitled Man in His Element, or A New Way to Keep House. The tale begins with a widowed sister and a woman's plan for running a household. Its humor turns on domestic order, or the lack of it, at Christmas time. Francis writes a light seasonal story for family reading.
betty-gordon-at-mountain-camp-or-the-mys:
Alice B. Emerson sent Betty Gordon to the mountains in this series volume from Cupples and Leon of New York. Betty, Bob, and their friends from Salsette Academy winter at a camp where snow rules the plot. The mystery of Ida Bellethorne — a vanished singer whose story haunts the camp — gives the volume its second title and its secret to solve.

One set piece has the quartette digging out through a snowbank. They slope a tunnel several yards long, tramping the snow hard beneath, and batter their way to the surface. It is great sport for the girls and work for the men, who would have quit without the young diggers' eagerness. Emerson keeps the Betty Gordon formula bright: outdoor adventure, a hidden identity, and mysteries solved by girls who refuse to be snowed in.
britannica-1911-a-she-ho: A-she-ho, also given as Alchuku in Manchu, is the subject of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry places the town in Manchuria, China, at a set distance north-east of Kirin and south of the Sungari river. A mandarin of the second class governs the town, the entry states. Its people are counted at about sixty thousand. The whole notice runs to a few lines, giving place, rule, and size for a treaty-era map of the region.
britannica-1911-arapaho:
Arapaho is a tribe of North American Indians. Their stock is Algonquian in language. The name may come from a Pawnee word. That word possibly means trader. They once ranged the central plains. The Platte and Arkansas rivers bounded their range. They were brave, warlike, and predatory. With Sioux and Cheyennes they fought the Utes. That warfare was unremitting for years.

Treaties divided the tribe geographically in 1867. Southern divisions went to Indian Territory reservations. That territory is now Oklahoma. Northern divisions settled in western Wyoming. The southern section sold its reservations in 1892. Its members became American citizens then. Total Arapaho numbers are about 2,000. Schoolcraft's tribal history is cited first. Hodge's Handbook of American Indians follows. The short entry relies on those authorities.
britannica-1911-ayacucho:
Ayacucho is a city and department of central Peru, once called Guamanga or Huamanga, renamed for the small plain of Ayacucho, Quichua for corner of death. On that plain in 1824 General Sucre beat the Spanish viceroy La Serna, a victory that won Peru its independence.

The city was founded by Pizarro in 1539. It stands on a high plateau between ranges, on the Lima to Cuzco road. Its people numbered 20,000 in 1896. Many churches, a bishopric, and a high court mark it. Its department crosses the old Inca homeland: cold heights growing corn and potatoes, warm valleys giving tropical fruits, and many silver mines at work. The name change came by decree in 1825.
britannica-1911-castello-branco-camillo-:
Castello Branco, Camillo is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Portuguese novelist. He grew up in a village in Traz-os-Montes, dreaming more than he read. He studied irregularly, tried journalism, then entered a seminary. From then on he kept up a feverish output of writing until the end.

The article sorts his work into kinds. There are romances of the imagination, novels of manners, and works of history and criticism. In all he published about two hundred and sixty books. The article praises his strongly marked national types, drawn from life he knew at first hand. Made a viscount in 1885, he died by his own hand in 1890.
britannica-1911-chuncho: Chuncho names a people of South American Indians treated in a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They live in the forests east of Cuzco, in central Peru. The entry calls them a fierce people who have kept their freedom from outside rule. They are said to be kin to their neighbours the Antis. They dwell in houses shared by many families and live chiefly by hunting. The name has also been used for one of the three native stocks of Peru, the other two being Quichua and Aymara.
britannica-1911-jericho:
Jericho was an important town in the Jordan valley, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces its place in the biblical record. It lies some five miles north of the Dead Sea. Its name is of disputed sense, perhaps meaning fragrant, or moon city.

The entry notes that the Pentateuch mentions it only in rough geography, but Joshua tells at length how it was the first Canaanite city attacked and taken by Israel. It casts doubt on total destruction, since a hamlet of Jericho still appears among the towns of Benjamin. Rebuilt by Hiel of Bethel, it later housed a school of prophets, and Elisha was said to have healed its bad waters.
britannica-1911-manetho:
Manetho was a priest and year man of Egypt, born in a town of the Delta. His name has a true ring of that land and shows on a sheet of his own days. Marks link him to the days of the first two Greek kings of Egypt. His chief work was a past of Egypt writ in Greek.

For that work he turned the home writs to the Greek tongue. The book lives just in bits in a foe work and in lists of kings with reign spans. Those lists are marred by faults in names, in rank, and in years. Yet they gave the frame of reign lines still used.
britannica-1911-poncho: Poncho is named in a 1911 Britannica article as a form of cloak from South America. The word is South American Spanish, taken from the Araucanian poncho or pontho in the seventeenth century. The cloak was worn first by the native peoples of South America. Spaniards living there later took it up as well. The hosted text opens with the tail of another article, on composer Ponchielli, before the poncho entry begins. What survives still fixes the garment's name, origin, and the two groups who wore it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ayacucho: Ayacucho, also called Guamanga, is a Peruvian diocese under Lima. Paul V erected the See of Guamanga on 20 July 1609. It stood vacant from 1821 to 1838, when it was transferred to Ayacucho. The diocese counts 200,610 Catholics, with 96 parishes, 120 secular priests, and 212 churches or chapels. No further history, bishop, or event is given beyond those dates and figures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-c:
This reference entry examines the councils of Clovesho, a place in the Anglo-Saxon Church whose exact site has never been pinned down. It weighs rival guesses, from Abingdon to Tewkesbury and Cliff-at-Hoo. Each guess, it concludes, rests on shaky ground, while the councils themselves and their acts are genuine.

The story starts with Archbishop Theodore's 673 decree that yearly synods meet at Clofeshoch. From there it follows the recorded councils through the eighth century, including debates over church privilege and discipline. The entry leans on Bede, Haddan and Stubbs, and other standard collections. It makes a useful guide to an early English church puzzle that still resists a tidy answer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giacomo-rho:
Giacomo Rho was a Jesuit missionary born at Milan in 1593, who died at Peking in 1638. Son of a noble jurist, he entered the Society of Jesus at twenty and, after weak early studies, grew strong in mathematics. Ordained at Rome by Cardinal Bellarmine, he sailed for the Far East in 1617 with forty-four companions. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces his path from Macao to the imperial court.

At Macao, during a Dutch siege, he taught the people to use artillery, and that service opened China to him. He quickly learned the language, and in 1631 the emperor called him to Peking to reform the Chinese calendar. With Father Schall he worked at that hard task until his death. Many Chinese officials attended his funeral, and he left writings on the calendar, astronomy, and theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-idaho:
Idaho, probably from an Arapaho word meaning Gem of the Mountains, was first suggested as a name for Colorado territory. A Pacific Slope state shaped roughly like a rudder, it stretches nearly five hundred miles south from Canada. It is bounded by Utah and Nevada, Oregon and Washington, Wyoming and Montana, and British Columbia. Its area exceeds eighty-three thousand square miles, a third of it government forest reserves.

Central Idaho is vast and mountainous, holding the Salmon River, Lost River, Sawtooth, Boise, Seven Devils, and other well-timbered ranges. Its mean elevation nears forty-seven hundred feet, with extremes from under eight hundred to over twelve thousand feet. The Bitter Root range, part of the Continental Divide, forms much of the eastern border, and the entry goes on to the state's climate, resources, people, and church history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jericho:
Jericho, the City of Palm Trees, appears here as three successive towns on neighbouring sites. The first, Canaanite Jericho, fell to Joshua after the Jordan crossing, later housed Benjamin's town, suffered under Moab's Eglon, sheltered David's envoys. It was rebuilt under Ahab by Hiel of Bethel.

Elisha purified its spring, exiles repopulated it after captivity, and Bacchides fortified it for Syria. Digs in 1907 and 1908 at Tell es-Sultan uncovered an 840-yard rampart, a double-walled citadel, kings' houses, and later Jewish pottery. The entry then follows Jericho's later towns down to the modern village near the spring.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-labarum-chi-r:
The labarum was the military standard Constantine the Great adopted after his vision of a cross of light. Eusebius pictures it as a long gold-covered spear with a crossbar, crowned by a wreath of gold and jewels holding the Chi-Rho, the interlaced first letters of Christ's name.

From the crossbar hung a square purple banner, rich with gems and gold, inscribed in Greek Touto nika, conquer by this sign, rendered in Latin as In hoc signo vinces. Medallions of the emperor and his children adorned the staff, and fifty picked guardsmen defended the standard. Similar standards went to all legions, the monogram was cut on shields, and coins show its changing forms, though the symbol itself predated Constantine's conversion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marcus-salviu:
Marcus Salvius Otho was Roman emperor after Galba and Nero, born at Rome on 28 April 32 and dead at Brixellum on the Po on 15 April 69. At Nero's court he lived loosely, and as husband of Poppaea Sabina he was posted to Lusitania as governor, for form's sake.

When Galba was proclaimed emperor, Otho returned with him to Rome. Against Galba's miserliness, Otho courted troops with gifts. On 15 January 69, five days after Galba named Piso his heir, twenty-three soldiers proclaimed Otho emperor in the street. Galba was murdered at the Forum, and the senate confirmed Otho. Vitellius, proclaimed at Cologne, marched from Germany with a third of the army behind him. Otho restored Nero's statues, recalled Nero's exiles, and put Tigellinus to death. He marched north on 14 March, lost near Cremona on 14 April before eastern legions joined him, and killed himself the next day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-agath:
Agatho was born in Sicily toward the end of the sixth century. He is believed to have lived as a Benedictine monk at Palermo's St Hermes. He was over one hundred when he took the papal chair in 678 as successor to Donus. Soon after, Wilfred of York came to Rome after Theodore of Canterbury deposed him unjustly. At a Lateran synod Agatho restored Wilfred to his see.

The chief event of his reign was the Sixth Ecumenical Council at Constantinople in 680. Papal legates presided, and the council practically ended the Monothelite heresy. Agatho died before its decrees reached Rome for his approval. He was buried in St Peter's on 10 January 681. He was famed for affability and charity, and for many miracles he is called Thaumaturgus, the Wonderworker.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zakho:
Zakho is a Chaldean diocese matching the ancient see of Maalta, once suffragan of Adiabene or Arbela. Nestorian bishops appear there from the fifth to the seventh century in Chabot's Synodicon Orientale. The see stayed joined to Akra and Amadia until the mid-nineteenth century, when the province split into three dioceses: Amadia, Zakho, and Akra-Zehbar, with Zakho dating from 1859. Today Zakho province belongs to the Mossul vilayet, and its city holds 2500 people, 1500 Jews and 100 Christians, on an island in the Little Khabour.

The diocese counts 3500 Catholics, ten resident priests, five religious of Saint Hormisdas's congregation, fifteen parishes or stations, twenty churches and chapels, and one primary school. Its small Catholic flock lives among a largely Jewish town population on the upper Tigris frontier.
doe-osti-17076220-development-of-an-ultr:
Daniel Orea, Hongbin Sun, Kevin Robb, and Joanna McFarlane of Oak Ridge National Laboratory built a tool to measure the speed of sound in molten salts, reported in September 2026. Molten salt reactors need that value to describe how the salt compresses and to complete the physics used in design and safety work. Direct measuring at reactor heat is hard.

Their ultrasonic pulse echo system sends a sound pulse down a quartz rod into the salt. The pulse reflects off the vessel bottom and returns, and travel time plus distance gives the speed. Room temperature water checks read 1519 meters per second against an accepted 1488. A lithium chloride potassium chloride mix was then measured at three temperatures up to 644 degrees, with speed falling as heat rose.
doe-osti-3002044-diversion-path-analysis:
Karen K. Hogue, Maggie M. Arno, and Peter Sobel of Oak Ridge National Laboratory propose a safeguards method in ORNL/SPR-2025/4250, dated October 2025. Their subject is material control and accounting, the bookkeeping that proves nuclear material has not been diverted. Liquid-fueled molten salt reactors are hard to track because the fuel itself flows through pipes and tanks as a hot liquid.

The authors adapt diversion path analysis, an older method that maps every route by which material could be taken. Walking those routes shows where measurements and controls must sit. The report lays out the steps so a reactor designer can build an accounting approach around them. It draws on Energy Department accounting rules and Nuclear Regulatory Commission safeguards practice. Designers of molten salt plants are the main audience.
doe-osti-3013661-studying-f-electron-con:
Garry Grubbs II of Missouri University of Science and Technology and Stephen Cooke of SUNY Purchase wrote this final report for award DE-SC0023242. It studies the role of f-electrons in thorium and uranium compounds. The team used rotational spectroscopy to map the shapes of actinide compounds in the gas phase. A laser ablation source fed a chirped-pulse Fourier transform microwave spectrometer.

The group recorded the first pure rotational spectrum of a uranium-bearing polyatomic compound, SUO2. They also characterized the mixed chalcogenides OThS and OCeS. They measured highly excited vibrational states in ThS up to v=17 and in HfS up to v=19. The precise constants give quantum chemistry a hard test. They show how actinides bond in ways that differ from transition metals and lanthanides.
doe-osti-3022912-ultra-wide-bandgap-lase:
LLNL abbreviated report LLNL-TR-2001233, by Lars Voss, summarizes Strategic Initiative 22-SI-003 on ultra-wide-bandgap, laser-addressable photoconductors. These devices act as light-triggered electrical switches. A laser pulse makes the material conduct, letting it close high-power circuits with precise timing. The lab and other government users need that capability, and commercial parts do not supply it.

The materials focus is gallium oxide and its aluminum alloys, semiconductors whose very wide bandgaps should hold off high voltages. The report's reference trail shows the underlying science problem: controlling defects and doping. Papers treat the E1 defect center in beta gallium oxide and heat treatments in hydrogen and argon. They also treat how carbon and hydrogen impurities limit n-type doping in aluminum gallium oxide. Those details decide whether a crystal insulates until the laser arrives.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DouglasMikeShow: A letter dated December 2, 1967 was written to Shelley Andrews of The Mike Douglas Show, the popular television talk program. The writer discusses a book about Lee Harvey Oswald that was about to be published, along with a related speaking trip. The author's name cannot be recovered from the garbled text, so the letter survives as an unsigned piece of a book publicity effort.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIRoweGaryThom: Warren Brown wrote a piece called The Strange Life of an FBI Informer about Gary Thomas Rowe, a man who informed for the Bureau. Rowe's double life, paid source inside violent circles, made his story worth a feature. The surviving record gives the author, title, and subject but no date or detail, so the article stands as a named profile of one informer's career.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HooversNotesKin: Martin Waldron reported for The New York Times that several books were planned on the Ray case, with the first due out the next week. James Earl Ray stood accused of killing Martin Luther King Jr., and publishers moved fast to tell his story. The surviving record gives the author, paper, and headline but no date in the evidence, so the piece stands as Times coverage of the coming Ray books.
how-to-tell-the-birds-from-the-flowers-a:
Robert Williams Wood, a Johns Hopkins physicist, wrote and illustrated How to Tell the Birds from the Flowers in 1907 as a manual of flornithology for beginners. Each page pairs a bird with a similar-sounding plant: the clover and the plover, the crow and the crocus, the parrot and the carrot, the hen and the lichen. Short verses explain the difference, badly on purpose.

The tern and turnip pair shows the method: cooked to a turn, the turnip may be inferred changed to the bird, while the tern is glad he is not in the pot. Wood's nonsense became a small classic of scientific humor, reprinted for a century and loved by naturalists with a weakness for puns.
podcast-dannyjones-FTCiHvay0ho:
Dan Thayer talks with Danny Jones about a hard childhood and a death row case. The episode title frames Thayer as an inmate explaining his early years. Their sample opens far from prison, with hurricane cleanup in Naples.

Thayer describes rich and poor areas hit by the same storm. From there the talk turns back to his youth and choices. Jones asks how early harm shaped later violence. The episode aims for an origin story, told plainly, for listeners who want to understand a condemned man's path rather than just his crime.
podcast-dannyjones-xEmVrE-qSho:
Matt LaCroix returns to Danny Jones with a newly found ancient text that he warns could destroy the church. The episode title quotes that warning. LaCroix studies old texts and lost history, and he treats this find as a bomb.

LaCroix lays out what the text says, where it was found, and who kept it hid, as he tells it. He argues its words clash with the church's core tale. Jones asks how scholars can test the find. Listeners get a bold claim made in full by its top voice. The library files the talk as an archive record, without a verdict.
podcast-joerogan-0H5LCLljJho:
Author Graham Hancock and geologist Randall Carlson join Joe Rogan for episode 872 of the Joe Rogan Experience. The pair are famed as a team for the claim that comet hits felled a high Ice Age culture. Carlson is a field man of rocks and floods.

Hancock and Carlson lay out the signs they read in stone and soil for a vast cataclysm. They argue the blow reset the human tale and left myths as its trace. Rogan gives the pair his long form to teach. Listeners get the core talk that built their fame. The library keeps the episode as a record of their stated case.
podcast-joerogan-ASYtDNoaeHo:
Author Lawrence Wright joins Joe Rogan to tell what he learned of Jim Jones by talking with the cult leader's sons. Wright is a Pulitzer-winning writer on faith and cults. Jones led the Peoples Temple to mass death in Guyana.

Wright tells how the sons' tales reshaped his grasp of their father and his hold on his flock. He shares what life was like for boys raised in the cult's core. Rogan asks how a man so mad drew so many. Listeners get a deep, sad tale told by a top hand. The library holds the segment as an archive record. Note: the older summary says Wright talked with Jones's followers; the title says his sons.
podcast-joerogan-FqMsJZ2SRHo:
Duncan Trussell marks a milestone with episode 2000 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Trussell, the comedian-philosopher who has appeared on the show more than almost anyone, was the natural pick for the landmark number. The visit feels like a reunion as much as an interview.

The two range over their usual shared ground: psychedelics, death, love, and the comedy inside all of it. Rogan looks back at how far the show has come since Trussell's early visits. For fans, the episode is a celebration entry, proof of how much of the show's heart lives in this one friendship.
podcast-joerogan-K9qF687OZho:
What former intelligence official Christopher Mellon thinks of Bob Lazar is the question in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Mellon, who served at the top of U.S. intelligence, helped bring military UFO videos to the public. Lazar is the famous Area 51 claimant. Their names rarely meet.

Rogan works through Mellon's measured public statements and what they imply about Lazar's decades-old story. The talk weighs insider caution against outsider certainty, and asks why officials speak so carefully on this subject. The segment is a short, sharp study in how disclosure figures judge each other's claims.
podcast-joerogan-NY3Zg37nIHo:
Magician David Blaine joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1527. Blaine is famous less for tricks than for endurance feats: buried, frozen, and starved in public view. Rogan, a fan of people who test limits, gives him a long and admiring hearing.

Blaine explains how he trains his body and mind to hold breath, bear cold, and stay calm when panic would kill him. Rogan asks what the feats cost him and why he keeps raising the stakes. The episode is a study in discipline disguised as a chat about magic, full of stories no stage show could hold.
podcast-joerogan-rz0g7kptNHo:
Episode 2078 of the Joe Rogan Experience is Duncan Trussell's later-era return, and the chemistry is unchanged. Trussell, by then a veteran guest, slips straight back into his cosmic comic mode. Rogan gives him the long leash his fans expect.

The talk wanders through troubled times with jokes about death, love, and the end of the world. Trussell finds warmth in dark subjects and turns fear into play. Rogan laughs hard and shares his own takes on aging and fame. It is comfort listening for fans: the Trussell charm, undimmed after hundreds of episodes.
podcast-tuckercarlson-8SwvBVKwBHo:
Former Senate aide Tara Reade tells Tucker Carlson how her life moved to Russia. Reade had accused Joe Biden of assault from his Senate years. Biden denied the claim, and her story drew hard scrutiny.

Reade says she feared arrest or worse if she stayed in America. She describes exile as the price of speaking out. Carlson presents her as a woman punished for an accusation. Listeners hear her full account in her own words. The episode suits those who want the claim heard whole, with its doubts left for them to weigh.
podcast-tuckercarlson-p7ZGf_QEyho:
Tucker Carlson reports on Gaza in a grave episode that calls the war there the holocaust of our time. The title also says Israel shut down the holiest site in Christendom. Carlson speaks in his own voice with a clear charge.

Carlson lays out the death toll as he reads it and the pain of Christians caught in the war. He argues the West looks away while a holy land is crushed. He names the leaders he blames for the silence. Listeners get his full case in one place. The library keeps the episode as a record of his stated view.
ramuntcho:
Ramuntcho, by Pierre Loti, in Henri Pene du Bois's English translation, opens on an autumn evening in the Pyrenean country near Spain. Sad curlews, heralds of autumn, flee in a gray squall. They cross the cold mouths of the Adour, the Nivelle, and the Bidassoa. Their cries ring the half-death of the year.

Ramuntcho walks alone on a moss-covered path in rope soles. Supple and silent, he climbs from far away. His goal is his isolated house in deep shade near the Spanish frontier. Around him the corn stands dead straw in the valleys, beeches and oaks shed their leaves, and the wet earth gives off an odorous damp.
rung-ho:
Talbot Mundy's Rung Ho, headed as a novel from 1914, is shown here at Chapter IX. It stands under a short verse asking God to speed the speaker's master and give him a lead in the line. Dawn is barely breaking at a little mission house. A flea-bitten gray pony is saddled by a sleepy groom and brought round from an open-sided thatch stable in the rear. The violet and mauve before the harsh yellow glare fade as a coppersmith bird starts its endless bong-bong-bong and monkeys chatter in a near baobab tree.

On the stroke of sunrise Rosemary McClean steps out, settles her sun-helmet, and mounts with no help. Dark rings beneath dark eyes show the work of heat and sleepless worry on a girl of twenty. The narrator says she should have graced the cool, rain-swept hills of Scotland.
the-excellence-of-the-rosary-conferences:
Rev. M. J. Frings's The Excellence of the Rosary gives conferences for devotions in honour of the Blessed Virgin, printed at New York with a 1912 copyright. Church approvals head the book: a censor's nihil obstat and the imprimatur of John Cardinal Farley, dated September 19, 1912. Contents move from the devotion's name and origin to its power, then walk through each prayer.

Sign of the cross, creed, Our Father, Hail Mary, and Glory Be each get a talk. Later heads weigh the rosary's form and its mysteries. Frings wrote for sodalities of the Virgin.
the-history-of-the-reign-of-ferdinand-an: William H. Prescott wrote History of the Reign of Ferdinand and Isabella, the Catholic, in three volumes, and the pages present are marked Vol. III. The contents of Volume III outline Part Second, chapter ten, on the Italian wars and the partition of Naples, following Gonsalvo de Cordova through Calabria, the storming of St. George, and the surrender of Tarento, then chapter eleven on the rupture with France. Only the title page and contents outline are present here.
the-history-of-university-education-in-m: Bernard C. Steiner, A.M., fellow in history, wrote The History of University Education in Maryland, in the Johns Hopkins University Studies in Historical and Political Science, ninth series, printed at Baltimore in March-April 1891. The same issue carries The Johns Hopkins University (1876-1891) by Daniel C. Gilman, president of the university. The contents list colonial attempts to found a college, the first and second University of Maryland, Cokesbury College, and other extinct colleges. Only the title page and contents are present here.
the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-volume-0:
Volume eight of Suetonius's Lives of the Twelve Caesars, in Alexander Thomson's translation revised by T. Forester, gives the life of Aulus Salvius Otho. His ancestors came from Ferentum and ranked among the most considerable families in Etruria. His grandfather, raised in Livia Augusta's household, became a senator through her favor but rose no higher than praetor.

His father Lucius Otho was so dearly loved by Tiberius, and resembled him so closely, that many believed Tiberius was his father. Lucius governed with strict severity, even executing soldiers under his own eyes for killing their generals during a revolt against Claudius. Suetonius sketches a family of favor and harsh discipline behind the short-lived emperor.
the-mirror-of-kong-ho:
Ernest Bramah's The Mirror of Kong Ho presents letters from Kong Ho, a Chinese gentleman living among the Westerners of London. A publisher's note calls the letters lively and amusing, written home to China. Kong Ho calls his hosts barbarians and finds endless food for thought in their aids to life, such as the motor car and the piano, both unknown in China at the time. His introduction addresses the 'estimable barbarian' who suggested printing the letters.

Kong Ho promises undeviating fidelity to what he directly observed, though he admits he may have misunderstood an involved allusion. He contrasts his care with travelers who loot Chinese palaces and then publish subtly imagined calumnies. Impartiality, he insists, sways his brush, and truth lurks within his inkpot. He asks that his host's own remarks be left unchanged, as a test and proof to readers.
the-mysteries-of-udolpho:
Ann Radcliffe's romance The Mysteries of Udolpho, interspersed with pieces of poetry as its title announces, is present here only in a contents list, so the Gothic tale itself does not appear. The list divides the novel into volumes, each with its own numbered chapters. Volume I runs to thirteen chapters and Volume II to twelve.

Volume III's list is cut short at Chapter VII in the pages shown, and a fourth volume is not reached. Nothing here names Emily, Montoni, or the castle of Udolpho, and no line of Radcliffe's prose is included. Only the scale of the work, four volumes of short numbered chapters, can be judged from this frame.
the-rover-boys-on-the-river-or-the-searc:
Ninth in its series, The Rover Boys on the River is subtitled The Search for the Missing Houseboat. Arthur Winfield's introduction greets that number with some wonder. Nine volumes struck him as a great many tales about one set of boys. The story itself is complete.

The contents follow the boys through plans for an outing. They say good-bye to Putnam Hall. Days at home follow before they board a houseboat. Flapp and Baxter plot mischief along the way. A queer captain adds to the trouble. Then the houseboat itself disappears. Later headings promise horse thieves and a search on the river. A rescue closes the book.
thomas-hariot-the-mathematician-the-phil:
Henry Stevens of Vermont built his life of Thomas Hariot chiefly from dormant materials, with notices of Hariot's associates. A modern note adds that Hariot worked out the law of refraction early, wrote to Kepler, and watched comets. His only printed works were a Virginia report and a posthumous algebra handbook.

Stevens calls Hariot the first historian of Virginia and traces the land from Ponce de Leon's Terra Florida onward. French planting, Spanish destruction, and Raleigh's English foothold all enter his research. Readers get biography mixed with bibliography and the early history of English Virginia.
